subtitle: Fast memory is small, big memory is slow. A cache makes the big slow one look fast by remembering what you just used.

hier.body:
Think of your desk, your bookshelf and the library across town. The desk is tiny but instant; the library holds everything but takes a trip. You keep what you need most on the desk. Computers do exactly this, because no memory is fast, large and cheap at once. They stack them: registers (sub-ns, bytes), cache (ns, KB–MB), main memory (≈100 ns, GB), disk/SSD (µs–ms, TB).

Why does it work? Because of locality: temporal (what you used you will use again) and spatial (what is near what you used will be used). The hierarchy moves data in blocks so neighbours come along. Each level is a cache for the one below, as the figure says. Looping over an array element by element is fast on a cache mainly because of spatial locality.
keynotes: No memory is fast, large and cheap at once, so computers stack registers (sub-ns, bytes), cache (ns, KB–MB), main memory (≈100 ns, GB) and disk/SSD (µs–ms, TB).
It works because of locality: temporal (what you used you will use again) and spatial (what is near what you used will be used).
The hierarchy moves data in blocks so neighbours come along.

mapping.body:
When a block comes into the cache, where may it sit? You have three choices. There are three answers. In exactly one line: direct-mapped, which is cheap, but blocks that map to the same line keep evicting each other (conflict misses). In any line: fully associative, which is flexible but expensive to search. In any line within one set: set-associative (e.g. 2-way), the usual compromise. An address splits into tag | index | offset; the index picks the set, the tag is compared with each line in it, the offset picks the byte.

Watch the same 5 addresses 0 8 0 6 8 into a 4-line cache: direct-mapped gets 5 misses, 2-way 4, fully associative 3. In the first figure, addresses 0 and 8 both map to line 0 and keep evicting each other; in the 2-way cache they coexist. Now size one: a 32-bit address, 4 KB direct-mapped cache with 16-byte blocks. Offset bits = log₂16 = 4. Lines = 4096/16 = 256, so index bits = 8, and the tag = 32 − 8 − 4 = 20 bits. That is why the direct-mapped cache misses on the second reference to address 0: address 8 evicted it.
keynotes: Direct-mapped places a block in exactly one line (cheap, but conflict misses); fully associative allows any line (flexible, expensive to search); set-associative allows any line within one set.
An address splits into tag | index | offset: the index picks the set, the tag is compared and the offset picks the byte.
Addresses 0 8 0 6 8 into a 4-line cache give 5 misses direct-mapped, 4 for 2-way and 3 fully associative.
A 32-bit address with a 4 KB direct-mapped cache and 16-byte blocks has 4 offset bits, 8 index bits and a 20-bit tag.

policy.body:
When the set is full and a new block arrives, someone has to leave. The replacement policy picks the victim: LRU (least recently used), FIFO, or random. And what about writes? Write-through updates memory every time (simple, slow; often with a write buffer). Write-back marks the line dirty and writes memory only on eviction (fast, but more complicated).

On a write miss you also choose: write-allocate loads the block first, while no-write-allocate writes straight to memory. What does a write-back cache save compared with write-through? Many memory writes: repeated updates to the same line cost one write on eviction.
keynotes: Replacement picks a victim when a set is full: LRU (least recently used), FIFO or random.
Write-through updates memory every time; write-back marks the line dirty and writes memory only on eviction.
On a write miss, write-allocate loads the block first and no-write-allocate writes straight to memory.

amat.body:
Is a cache worth it? Let’s put a number on it. Average memory access time: AMAT = hit time + miss rate × miss penalty. With a 1-cycle hit, a 100-cycle penalty and the fully associative run above (40% hits, so a miss rate of 0.6), AMAT is 1 + 0.6 × 100 = 61 cycles. A cache with a 90% hit rate would give 1 + 0.1 × 100 = 11. Same machine, a very different story.

Multi-level caches nest the formula: the L1 miss penalty is the L2 access time. The AMAT of the fully associative run appears in the figure’s results. Try one yourself: hit time 2 ns, miss rate 5%, miss penalty 80 ns gives 2 + 0.05 × 80 = 6 ns.
keynotes: AMAT = hit time + miss rate × miss penalty.
With a 1-cycle hit, a 100-cycle penalty and 40% hits AMAT is 61 cycles; a 90% hit rate gives 1 + 0.1 × 100 = 11.
Multi-level caches nest the formula: the L1 miss penalty is the L2 access time.

ext.body:
What is memory physically made of? SRAM (flip-flops) is fast and used for caches. DRAM (a capacitor plus a transistor, refreshed constantly) is denser and used for main memory, in DDR DIMM/SODIMM modules. ROM and flash hold firmware. Externally you have magnetic disk, SSD, optical and tape; RAID levels 1–5 add redundancy (see the OS course for a worked RAID 5 parity example).

Why does DRAM need refreshing? Because the charge on its tiny capacitor leaks away, so every cell must be rewritten again and again.
keynotes: SRAM (flip-flops) is fast and used for caches; DRAM (a capacitor plus transistor, refreshed constantly) is denser and used for main memory.
External memory includes magnetic disk, SSD, optical and tape; RAID levels 1–5 add redundancy.

summary.body:
Three lines, and you can explain any cache.

  • Locality makes a small fast memory effective.
  • Direct, set-associative and fully associative trade cost against conflict misses.
  • AMAT = hit + miss rate × penalty.
keynotes: Locality makes a small fast memory effective.
Direct, set-associative and fully associative mappings trade cost against conflict misses.
AMAT = hit time + miss rate × penalty.
